Let $V$ be a complex vector space. A **formal distribution** in variables $z,w$ with coefficients in a complex vector space $E$ is an arbitrary coefficient family
$$F(z,w)=\sum_{p,q\in\mathbb Z}F_{p,q}z^pw^q,\qquad F_{p,q}\in E.$$
No convergence or summability is assumed. Multiplication by a polynomial in $z,w$ is defined coefficientwise; each resulting coefficient is a finite sum. The residue $\operatorname{Res}_z F$ is the coefficient of $z^{-1}$, retaining the other variables and coefficients. For a one-variable series $f(z)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}f_mz^m$, write $\operatorname{Res}_z f=f_{-1}$, in the same support convention as [[def-formal-laurent-series-and-residue]].

The **formal delta distribution** is
$$\delta(z,w)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}z^{-n-1}w^n.$$
For each integer $r$, the two binomial expansions of $(z-w)^r$ are
$$\iota_{z,w}(z-w)^r=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom rj(-1)^jz^{r-j}w^j,\qquad \iota_{w,z}(z-w)^r=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom rjz^j(-w)^{r-j},$$
where $\binom rj=r(r-1)\cdots(r-j+1)/j!$ and $\binom r0=1$. The first expansion is in nonnegative powers of $w$ and the second is in nonnegative powers of $z$; they are distinct when $r<0$.

A formal distribution $A(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_nz^{-n-1}$ with $A_n\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ is a **field on $V$** if for every $v\in V$ there is an integer $N(v,A)$ such that $A_nv=0$ for all $n\ge N(v,A)$. Equivalently, $A(z)v\in V((z))$: its powers of $z$ are bounded below, as in [[def-formal-laurent-series-and-residue]], with coefficients in $V$. Define its modes by $A_{(n)}=A_n=\operatorname{Res}_z z^nA(z)$.

Two fields $A(z),B(w)$ are **mutually local** if some integer $N\ge0$ satisfies $(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0$ as a formal distribution, where $[A(z),B(w)]=A(z)B(w)-B(w)A(z)$. For any integer $n$, their **$n$th product field** is
$$A(z)_{(n)}B(z)=\operatorname{Res}_x\Bigl(\iota_{x,z}(x-z)^nA(x)B(z)-\iota_{z,x}(x-z)^nB(z)A(x)\Bigr).$$
These conventions use ordinary, ungraded vector spaces and ordinary commutators; no super sign is implicit.

Since $\operatorname{Res}_z(z^m\delta(z,w))=w^m$, differentiation gives $\operatorname{Res}_z(z^m\partial_w^j\delta/j!)=\binom mj w^{m-j}$ for every integer $m$. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex Lie algebra, and let $T(\mathfrak g)=\bigoplus_{n\ge 0}\mathfrak g^{\otimes n}$ be its tensor algebra. Let $I\subseteq T(\mathfrak g)$ be the two-sided ideal generated by all elements

$$x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y] \qquad (x,y\in \mathfrak g).$$

$$U(\mathfrak g):=T(\mathfrak g)/I.$$

The image of $x\in \mathfrak g$ in $U(\mathfrak g)$ is again denoted by $x$. The defining relation is therefore

$$xy-yx=[x,y] \qquad (x,y\in \mathfrak g).$$

This is the quotient algebra used throughout the page for PBW, the Casimir element, and the Harish-Chandra projection.

derivations.claim: Fix a finite ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $\mathfrak g$ and the countable basis $e_{i,n}=e_i\otimes t^n$ of the loop modes, together with $K$. Fix a total order on this basis that places every mode with $n<0$ before every basis element of $\mathfrak p$; within each part use any fixed enumeration. For basis letters $b_j>b_i$, apply the defining rewrite $b_jb_i\mapsto b_ib_j+[b_j,b_i]$. Order words by length and then inversion number. The swapped word has one fewer inversion and every bracket term has smaller length; each bracket is a finite linear combination of basis letters. Thus every reduction tree is finitely branching and strictly decreases this well-founded pair, so it terminates in a finite linear combination of ordered words.

Reductions at disjoint adjacent pairs commute. The only overlapping reductions occur in a descending triple $xyz$ of basis letters with $x>y>z$. Reducing the left pair first and then swapping the remaining inversions gives
$$xyz\longrightarrow zyx+[y,z]x+y[x,z]+[x,y]z,$$
whereas reducing the right pair first gives
$$xyz\longrightarrow zyx+z[x,y]+[x,z]y+x[y,z].$$
Their difference is $([y,z]x-x[y,z])+(y[x,z]-[x,z]y)+([x,y]z-z[x,y])$. By bilinearity, the two-letter defining relations reduce these three differences respectively to $[\,[y,z],x\,]$, $[y,[x,z]]$, and $[\,[x,y],z\,]$; their sum is zero by Jacobi. Each bracket expands into finitely many basis letters, and every comparison term has smaller word length than the original triple. Induction on (length, inversion number) therefore joins every overlapping reduction, also inside any fixed left and right word context, so all reduction paths from each word agree.

The resulting linear normal-form map fixes every ordered word and sends each contextual relation $u(b_jb_i-b_ib_j-[b_j,b_i])v$ to zero, by the uniqueness in step 1.2. This checks all basis pairs: a reversed pair is the negative of its oriented relation by antisymmetry, and an equal pair has bracket zero. Bilinearity then gives the same for arbitrary $x,y\in\widehat{\mathfrak g}$, so the map kills the full two-sided ideal $I$ of [F2]. Conversely each reduction changes a word by an element of $I$. Hence ordered monomials span the quotient, and a linear combination of distinct ordered monomials in $I$ would be fixed by the normal-form map and also sent to zero; it must be zero. Ordered monomials are therefore a basis of $U(\widehat{\mathfrak g})$.

The negative-mode span $\mathfrak n_-:=\mathfrak g\otimes t^{-1}\mathbb C[t^{-1}]$ is a Lie subalgebra because sums of two negative indices stay negative and [F1] has no central term for them. The subalgebra $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak g[t]\oplus\mathbb CK$ is established in [F4]. With the order fixed in step 1.1, each PBW word is a negative-mode monomial followed by a $U(\mathfrak p)$-monomial. Thus multiplication identifies $U(\mathfrak n_-)\otimes U(\mathfrak p)$ with $U(\widehat{\mathfrak g})$ as a vector space and as a right $U(\mathfrak p)$-module.

Tensor the right-module decomposition in step 3.1 over $U(\mathfrak p)$ with $\mathbb C_k$. It identifies [F3] with $U(\mathfrak n_-)\otimes\mathbb C_k$; the negative-mode PBW monomials tensor the nonzero generator of $\mathbb C_k$ to a basis. The empty monomial is nonzero, proving the claimed basis and vacuum assertion.

The residue $\operatorname{Res}_z F$ is the coefficient of $z^{-1}$, retaining the other variables and coefficients. For a one-variable series $f(z)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}f_mz^m$, write $\operatorname{Res}_z f=f_{-1}$, in the same support convention as [[def-formal-laurent-series-and-residue]].

The **formal delta distribution** is
$$\delta(z,w)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}z^{-n-1}w^n.$$
For each integer $r$, the two binomial expansions of $(z-w)^r$ are
$$\iota_{z,w}(z-w)^r=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom rj(-1)^jz^{r-j}w^j,\qquad \iota_{w,z}(z-w)^r=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom rjz^j(-w)^{r-j},$$
where $\binom rj=r(r-1)\cdots(r-j+1)/j!$ and $\binom r0=1$. The first expansion is in nonnegative powers of $w$ and the second is in nonnegative powers of $z$; they are distinct when $r<0$.

A formal distribution $A(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_nz^{-n-1}$ with $A_n\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ is a **field on $V$** if for every $v\in V$ there is an integer $N(v,A)$ such that $A_nv=0$ for all $n\ge N(v,A)$. Equivalently, $A(z)v\in V((z))$: its powers of $z$ are bounded below, as in [[def-formal-laurent-series-and-residue]], with coefficients in $V$. Define its modes by $A_{(n)}=A_n=\operatorname{Res}_z z^nA(z)$.

Two fields $A(z),B(w)$ are **mutually local** if some integer $N\ge0$ satisfies $(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0$ as a formal distribution, where $[A(z),B(w)]=A(z)B(w)-B(w)A(z)$. For any integer $n$, their **$n$th product field** is
$$A(z)_{(n)}B(z)=\operatorname{Res}_x\Bigl(\iota_{x,z}(x-z)^nA(x)B(z)-\iota_{z,x}(x-z)^nB(z)A(x)\Bigr).$$
These conventions use ordinary, ungraded vector spaces and ordinary commutators; no super sign is implicit.

derivations.claim: Let $V=\mathbb C^2$ with basis $v_1,v_2$. Define constant fields $A(z)=E_{12}$ and $B(w)=E_{21}$, where $E_{12}v_2=v_1$, $E_{12}v_1=0$, $E_{21}v_1=v_2$, and $E_{21}v_2=0$. Their only nonzero modes are $A_{(-1)}=E_{12}$ and $B_{(-1)}=E_{21}$, so both are fields by [F1].

Their commutator is $[A(z),B(w)]=E_{11}-E_{22}\ne0$. For every integer $N\ge0$, $(z-w)^N(E_{11}-E_{22})$ has nonzero coefficient $z^N(E_{11}-E_{22})$, including $N=0$. Thus no locality exponent exists, although both fields are lower-truncated; the refuted implication fails.

boundaries.reason: The counterexample uses V=C2 and two explicit fields, rather than an empty pair family.

boundaries.evidence: At locality exponent N=0 the commutator remains E11-E22!=0, already violating locality. Zero high modes do not imply locality.
Each field has only its mode -1 nonzero, providing the smallest finite-mode truncation witness.
The lower-truncation property survives despite noncommuting constant matrices, showing no analytic completion issue is responsible.
The exponent boundary N=0 is explicitly included in 2.1, and all N>=0 fail by the z^N coefficient.

boundaries.reason: The two matrix units are explicit, so no vector, basis family or exponent is selected to construct the witness.
The example refutes a one-way implication from truncation to locality.
It does not deny the separately imposed locality axiom or assert a converse equivalence.

A (non-super) **vertex algebra** over $\mathbb C$ is a complex vector space $V$ equipped with a nonzero vector $\mathbf1\in V$, a linear operator $T:V\to V$, and a linear **state–field map**
$$Y(-,z):V\longrightarrow (\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V))^{\mathbb Z},\qquad a\longmapsto Y(a,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{(n)}z^{-n-1},$$
where the codomain denotes all endomorphism-valued coefficient families indexed by $\mathbb Z$.
satisfying the following axioms.

1. **Field and truncation.** For each $a,v\in V$, there is an integer $N(a,v)$ such that $a_{(n)}v=0$ for all $n\ge N(a,v)$. Thus $Y(a,z)v\in V((z))$ in the lower-bounded support sense of [[def-formal-laurent-series-and-residue]].

2. **Vacuum and creation.** $Y(\mathbf1,z)=\operatorname{id}_V$, $T\mathbf1=0$, and
   $$Y(a,z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}a:=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{z^rT^r a}{r!}.$$
   This is a formal power series; no analytic convergence is asserted.

3. **Translation covariance.** For every $a\in V$,
   $$[T,Y(a,z)]=\partial_zY(a,z).$$

4. **Locality.** For every $a,b\in V$, some integer $N\ge0$ satisfies
   $$(z-w)^N[Y(a,z),Y(b,w)]=0.$$

The coefficient $a_{(n)}b$ is called the $n$th product of the states $a,b$. The mode and formal-distribution conventions in [[def-formal-distribution-on-a-vector-space]] are in force. The axioms are algebraic and do not impose a grading, conformal vector, simplicity, unitarity, or analytic OPE convergence.

derivations.claim: If $a=0$, then $e^{zT}a=0$; otherwise let $d=\deg a$, so $T^ra=0$ for $r>d$ and $e^{zT}a$ is a polynomial in $z$. Hence $Y(a,z)b$ has finite support in nonnegative powers for every $b$, and its coefficients define a field. Direct substitution gives $Y(1,z)b=b$ and $Y(a,z)1=e^{zT}a$. Also $T1=0$.
For any $b\in V$, the derivation law in [A1] gives $[T,Y(a,z)]b=T((e^{zT}a)b)-(e^{zT}a)Tb=(T e^{zT}a)b=\partial_zY(a,z)b$, so translation covariance holds.

Each $Y(a,z)$ acts by multiplication by $e^{zT}a$. Multiplication operators commute because $V$ is commutative, so $[Y(a,z),Y(c,w)]=0$ for every $a,c\in V$. Thus locality holds with exponent $N=0$. All axioms of [F1] are verified.

boundaries.evidence: For a=0 the exponential field is zero without assigning a degree to the zero polynomial (1.1).
The positive-degree derivatives eventually vanish, and the locality exponent can be 0 because all multiplication fields commute (3.1).
The vacuum is 1 and Y(1,z)b=b, while T1=0 and Y(a,z)1=e^(zT)a are checked in 1.1.
Constant polynomials give constant multiplication fields and zero derivative, included in the same finite exponential.
The exponential starts at r=0 and terminates at deg a for nonzero a. There is no analytic endpoint limit.

boundaries.reason: Polynomial differentiation and multiplication give every coefficient explicitly, without a choice of truncation representatives.
The example verifies the listed vertex axioms for C[u] directly.
It does not assert that all vertex algebras arise from commutative differential algebras.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra, let $B$ be the normalized invariant form of [[def-untwisted-affine-central-extension]], and let $k\in\mathbb C$. The induced module $V^k(\mathfrak g)$ of [[def-universal-affine-vacuum-module]] has a unique vertex-algebra structure in the convention of [[def-vertex-algebra-state-field]] for which $\mathbf1$ is the vacuum and
$$Y(x_{-1}\mathbf1,z)=J^x(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}x_nz^{-n-1}\qquad(x\in\mathfrak g).$$
This construction is valid for every complex level, including values at which a normalized Sugawara denominator vanishes. It asserts no conformal vector, simple quotient, unitarity, or integrability.

Write $\mathfrak{gl}_2(\mathbb C)=M_2(\mathbb C)$ for the Lie algebra of
complex $2\times2$ matrices under the commutator bracket
$[A,B]=AB-BA$ ([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]],
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]). The **special linear Lie algebra**
$\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ is the Lie subalgebra
([[def-lie-subalgebra-ideal-and-center]]) of traceless matrices

$$\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_2(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\},$$

which is closed under the bracket because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$. Put

$$e=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad f=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad h=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Direct matrix multiplication gives $he-eh=2e$, $hf-fh=-2f$ and
$ef-fe=h$, that is,

$$[h,e]=2e,\qquad [h,f]=-2f,\qquad [e,f]=h .$$

Since $\{e,f,h\}$ is a basis of the space of traceless matrices, these
relations determine the bracket completely, $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ is
three-dimensional, and $h$ spans a one-dimensional abelian subalgebra.
A Lie algebra over $\mathbb C$ is called a **copy of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$** if it
has a basis $(e,f,h)$ satisfying exactly these three bracket relations.

Use [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]]. Fix the positive-real rescaling $B$ of the Killing form whose induced form on the real finite-root span makes every long root have square $2$. The Killing form is nondegenerate, invariant and symmetric by [[lem-finite-lie-engel-trace-criterion-and-killing-nondegeneracy]], and its restriction gives a positive definite real root form by [[lem-finite-semisimple-cartan-root-and-string-structure]], so this rescaling exists. In particular $B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z])$.

For $f=\sum_m a_mt^m$ put $f'=\sum_m ma_mt^{m-1}$ and $\operatorname{Res}(f\,dt)=a_{-1}$. Define the residue bilinear form by
$$\omega(x\otimes f,y\otimes q)=B(x,y)\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt).$$
The formula is balanced and complex bilinear, so extends uniquely to the tensor product. In particular,
$$\omega(x_m,y_n)=m\delta_{m,-n}B(x,y).$$
The Kronecker symbol is one when $m=-n$ and zero otherwise. This form is in fact an alternating Lie-algebra two-cocycle. For Laurent polynomials $f,q$, the residue of $(fq)'$ is zero, so $\operatorname{Res}(f'q\,dt)=-\operatorname{Res}(fq'\,dt)$; symmetry of $B$ gives skew-symmetry, and in characteristic zero also $\omega(a,a)=0$. For pure tensors $x\otimes f,y\otimes q,z\otimes h$, invariance and symmetry of $B$ make the three factors $B([x,y],z)$, $B([y,z],x)$, and $B([z,x],y)$ equal. The cyclic cocycle sum is therefore that common factor times
$$\operatorname{Res}\bigl(((fq)'h+(qh)'f+(hf)'q)\,dt\bigr)=2\operatorname{Res}((fqh)'\,dt)=0.$$
Trilinearity extends the identity to all loop-algebra elements. Thus the terminology “two-cocycle” records a proved property of the defined form, not merely an intended later use.

For any long root $\alpha$, opposite root vectors normalized by $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=\alpha^\vee$ satisfy
$$B(e_\alpha,f_\alpha)=\frac{2}{(\alpha,\alpha)}=1.$$
The equality follows by pairing $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]$ with the Cartan and using invariance. A later result identifies the highest root and proves that it is long; no highest-root existence claim is used here.

For a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ as in [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], use the invariant form $B$ normalized by long roots of square $2$ in [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. By [[lem-adjoint-casimir-is-positive-scalar]], the Casimir $\Omega_B$ from [[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] acts in the adjoint representation as $\gamma_B I$ for a unique positive real scalar $\gamma_B$. Define the **dual Coxeter number** by $h^\vee=\gamma_B/2$. Thus, for a $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$-orthonormal basis of a compact real form from [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]], $-\sum_i\operatorname{ad}(X_i)^2=2h^\vee I$; this is the normalization used in the affine central term and every Sugawara denominator below.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra as in [[def-loop-algebra-of-a-simple-lie-algebra]], with normalized invariant form $B$ from [[def-untwisted-affine-central-extension]]. Let $\rho$ be a restricted affine-current module of level $k$ as in [[def-positive-energy-affine-module]], and assume $k+h^\vee\ne0$ for the number in [[def-dual-coxeter-number-for-normalized-form]]. Choose any $B$-dual bases $(x_a)$ and $(x^a)$ of $\mathfrak g$. Write $J_x(n)=\rho(x\otimes t^n)$.

For modes, define
$$:J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(s):=\begin{cases}J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(s),&r<0,\\J_{x^a}(s)J_{x_a}(r),&r\ge0.\end{cases}$$
The **Sugawara mode** of index $m\in\mathbb Z$ is
$$L_m=\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_a\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{x_a}(r)J_{x^a}(m-r):.$$
For the compact real form of [[def-compact-real-form-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]], put $Q=-B|_{\mathfrak k}$; it is positive by the normalized form in [[def-residue-two-cocycle-on-a-loop-algebra]]. If $(X_i)$ is $Q$-orthonormal, then $( -X_i)$ is its $B$-dual, so the same formula reads
$$L_m=-\frac{1}{2(k+h^\vee)}\sum_i\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}:J_{X_i}(r)J_{X_i}(m-r):.$$
By [[lem-sugawara-quadratic-modes-well-defined]], the mode sum is locally finite on every vector and independent of the chosen dual bases. At the **critical level** $k=-h^\vee$ the scalar denominator is zero and this normalized formula is not defined; no operator is asserted there.

Let $V^k(\mathfrak g)$ be the vacuum module of [[def-universal-affine-vacuum-module]], with $\mathfrak g$ finite-dimensional complex simple and $k\in\mathbb C$. Then for every $x\in\mathfrak g$,
$$J^x(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}x_nz^{-n-1}$$
is a field, is creative with $J^x(z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}(x_{-1}\mathbf1)$, and is translation-covariant. For $x,y\in\mathfrak g$,
$$[J^x(z),J^y(w)]=J^{[x,y]}(w)\delta(z,w)+kB(x,y)\partial_w\delta(z,w),$$
so the current fields are pairwise local of order at most $2$, with formal OPE
$$J^x(z)J^y(w)\sim\frac{J^{[x,y]}(w)}{z-w}+\frac{kB(x,y)\operatorname{id}}{(z-w)^2}.$$

derivations.claim: Since $-2\in\mathbb C$, [F1] gives the universal affine vertex algebra at this level; its construction does not divide by $k+h^\vee$.

By [F2] and [F3], invariance gives $B(h,h)=B([e,f],h)=B(e,[f,h])=2$. It also gives $B(h,e)=B(h,f)=B(e,e)=B(f,f)=0$: for example $2B(e,e)=B([h,e],e)=B(h,[e,e])=0$, and $2B(h,e)=B([h,e],h)=-B(e,[h,h])=0$; the $f$ identities follow from $[h,f]=-2f$ in the same way. Thus the $B$-dual basis to $(h,e,f)$ is $(h/2,f,e)$. The adjoint Casimir is therefore $\Omega_B=\tfrac12\operatorname{ad}(h)^2+\operatorname{ad}(e)\operatorname{ad}(f)+\operatorname{ad}(f)\operatorname{ad}(e)$. On $h$ its last two terms give $2h+2h=4h$; on $e$ its first two nonzero terms give $2e+2e=4e$; on $f$ its first and last nonzero terms give $2f+2f=4f$. Hence $\gamma_B=4$ and [F4] gives $h^\vee=2$.
Applying [F6] to $x=e,y=f$, with $[e,f]=h$, $B(e,f)=1$, and $k=-2$, gives the stated current OPE.

At $k=-2$ and $h^\vee=2$, the denominator in [F5] is $2(-2+2)=0$. Therefore this normalized Sugawara expression is undefined, even though step 1.1 supplies the affine vertex algebra. No Sugawara or Virasoro structure is inferred.

boundaries.reason: The sl2 vacuum algebra has its nonzero PBW vacuum and is not an empty-mode carrier.

boundaries.evidence: The zero boundary is the normalized denominator 2(-2+2)=0, not a zero level or a failure of vertex-algebra existence.
The OPE single-pole coefficient is J^h and double-pole coefficient -2*id, preserving the nonzero vacuum identity.
Critical level -2 is deliberately allowed in the affine vertex algebra but excluded from the normalized Sugawara formula (1.1, 2.1).

boundaries.reason: The example concerns a critical algebraic scalar, without an analytic limiting approach to it.
The sl2 basis, dual, Casimir action and OPE coefficients are computed explicitly, without selecting alternative stress tensors.
The comparison separates two existence assertions and is not an iff characterization.
Undefined normalized Sugawara modes do not imply nonexistence of the affine vertex algebra or every alternative conformal construction.
